Document.alternatives: One class per artifact kind: rejected, union ranges everywhere and a vocabulary change per new kind. A Stage class: deferred to the workflow-vocabulary interview.
Document.question: Which document says so, and is it still current? Which artifacts describe the product, at which stage? (C4, D3, failure F2)
Document.why: Every fact cites a document, and a newer document supersedes an older one through the temporal vocabulary; kind and stage as attributes keep one class for all artifacts.

Tool.question: What can be done about this, and how?
Tool.why: The binding between an entity, the tool that acts on it, its inputs, its credentials by name and its preconditions is otherwise tribal knowledge in an agent's prompt; as a fact it is versioned, reviewed and shared. OTO never invokes it.
Tool.alternatives: A list of scripts beside the project. It cannot say what each acts on, when it is ready, or what its run proved. Called Action until 2026-10; Tool is MCP's word for the same shape.

Product.alternatives: A specific software-product class with releases and environments baked in; rejected because the user chose a generic vocabulary reused per project. Stage, domain and value stream moved to the portfolio on 2026-10-07: where a product stands is the executive's question.
Product.question: Why does this product exist, and what is it? (A1)
Product.why: The root the whole vocabulary hangs off. Generic on purpose: one vocabulary every project starts from, a product being whatever the project sets out to build.

Role.question: Who owns it and who decides? (PF1, PF5, PF6)
Role.why: Ownership questions are answered better by a role than a person, because roles are stable while people move; one Role at every level.
Role.alternatives: Role plus Person: rejected, no question needs a named individual's decisions traced.

Team.question: Which teams exist, what does each own, with what mandate? (PF6)
Team.why: The estate and the work are owned by teams; the product by roles. Declared once here so a project composing four packs has one Team.
Team.alternatives: Team as a kind of Role: rejected, a function and a group of people answer different pages.

Objective.question: What are we trying to achieve this period, and which products pursue it? (PF2)
Objective.why: The executive's objective and the product's are one thing; the product's success criteria measure it.
Objective.alternatives: A separate company objective class: rejected, `supports` already records the alignment between levels of objective.

Capability.question: Which capabilities do we need, which product provides each, and which has no product? (PF4)
Capability.why: What the business asks about in its own words; the gap between needed and provided is the portfolio's finding.
Capability.alternatives: Keeping Capability in the estate only: rejected, a capability is needed before any system enables it.

Assumption.alternatives: Merged into Constraint or Risk: rejected, an assumption is a belief to check, not a limit or a threat.
Assumption.question: What assumptions is it built under, and which could invalidate the plan? (B4)
Assumption.why: An assumption is validated or invalidated over time and decisions rest on it, so its state change must propagate; that needs a node with history.

Constraint.alternatives: One Concern class with a kind attribute: rejected, constraints, assumptions and risks have different lifecycles and owners.
Constraint.question: What constraints is it built under? (B4)
Constraint.why: A constraint is imposed from outside and limits requirements and releases; it has a source and a lifecycle distinct from an assumption or a risk.

Decision.alternatives: Decision as a status on the thing decided: rejected, no reason and no history.
Decision.question: What did we decide about X, when, and why? (C1, failure F1)
Decision.why: A decision has a date, a reason, evidence and a role that made it; a status field has none of those, and an agent needs to see a settled decision before reopening it.

Feature.alternatives: Epic and Story: rejected, Story is a delivery unit and ties the product model to one method. Capability: same thing, the user kept the name Feature.
Feature.question: What is the product made of? (D4)
Feature.why: Builders decompose the product into user-visible capabilities, each traced to a requirement; nesting through part_of lets epics and sub-features share one class.

JourneyStep.alternatives: Steps as an ordered list attribute: rejected, nothing can point at a step. Adding Screen: deferred to the design-vocabulary interview.
JourneyStep.question: How does a user get value, step by step? (D1)
JourneyStep.why: A step has identity of its own: a design decision, a requirement or a test points at one step, which a list attribute on the journey cannot support.

OpenQuestion.alternatives: Decisions with state = open: rejected, populated differently. Hotspot class: deferred until the method runs gates on contested areas.
OpenQuestion.question: What is still open or unresolved? (C2)
OpenQuestion.why: An open question is raised before any reason or evidence exists and is later resolved by a decision; keeping it separate lets an agent list what is open before building.

Persona.alternatives: Separate AntiPersona class: rejected, nothing points at it so it stays thin. Audience as a text attribute of Product: rejected, D1 and D2 lose their anchor.
Persona.question: Who is it for, and who is it not for? (A2)
Persona.why: Journeys, requirements and value propositions need something to point at, and the excluded audience must be a dated first-class fact, not a footnote.

Policy.alternatives: Policy as a Constraint kind: rejected, authority and scope differ. GovernanceBody class: deferred to the workflow vocabulary.
Policy.question: Which rules must the product obey, who enforces them, and what is affected? (G6; Gate 3 review)
Policy.why: A policy prescribes behaviour and has an authority and an enforcing role, which a budget or timeline constraint does not; two people would populate a shared class differently.

Release.alternatives: Requirement.scope attribute: rejected, nothing to be in scope of, B1 and C3 unanswerable. A Scope node per release: rejected, the edges already carry it.
Release.question: What is in and out of scope for the next release, and what was the scope as of a past date? (B1, C3)
Release.why: Scope has to be scope OF something dated; edges to a release carry validFrom and validTo, so the boundary at any past date is readable.

Requirement.alternatives: Folding requirements into Feature: rejected, a need and the capability that satisfies it have different owners and dates.
Requirement.question: What must the product do? What is in scope for the next release? (B3, B1)
Requirement.why: The unit a builder agent works from and a release scopes; it carries priority and kind, traces to a value proposition, and is what decisions are about.

Risk.alternatives: A fourth Dependency class: rejected, no question yet traverses to external systems or partners. Add it when one does.
Risk.question: What are the risks and external dependencies? (E1)
Risk.why: A risk threatens something, is mitigated by something, and can block a release; an external dependency is modelled as a risk kind because what matters is what happens if it fails.

Scenario.alternatives: UseCase class: rejected for now, a use case is a functional Requirement with its flow. Workflow class: rejected, a workflow is a UserJourney whose persona is a role.
Scenario.question: What exactly must this do in this situation, and how do we test it? (G5; Gate 3 review)
Scenario.why: A scenario is the concrete path tests and acceptance run on, with its own preconditions and expected result; it must be pointable from a test and a requirement.

SuccessCriterion.alternatives: List attribute on ValueProposition: rejected, no history, no owner, which is exactly F4. Measurement class for observed readings: deferred until a question asks for readings.
SuccessCriterion.question: How do we know the product succeeded? (B2, failure F4)
SuccessCriterion.why: A target that changes needs history and an owner, and a product with none must be flaggable; an attribute list gives neither.

Term.alternatives: Lexicon only: rejected, no citable definition. Term with a Domain grouping class: rejected, only if one word means two things in two contexts of one product.
Term.question: What does this word mean here, who said so, and has the meaning changed? (G7; Gate 3 review)
Term.why: A definition needs a citation and a date so a changed meaning is superseded, which the search lexicon cannot hold; the lexicon is generated from terms instead.

UserJourney.alternatives: Journey as text on Persona: rejected, nothing could reference it.
UserJourney.question: How does a user get value, step by step? (D1)
UserJourney.why: Design and tests must follow the same path; the journey is the path, owned by a persona and delivering a value proposition.

ValueProposition.alternatives: Separate Problem class: rejected, no question traverses from problem to several propositions. Attributes on Product: rejected, nothing could trace to a purpose.
ValueProposition.question: Why does it exist, and what is the value proposition in one sentence? Which requirement serves which purpose? (A1, A3, D2)
ValueProposition.why: It is the traceability anchor: requirements, journeys and criteria trace to it, so an orphan requirement (failure F3) becomes a rule violation instead of folklore.

Asset.alternatives: Naming the four classes in every question and rule; rejected because a question such as "what does the payments team own" has to be asked four times, and a rule about ownership written four times.
Asset.question: What do we run, and who is accountable for it?
Asset.why: Ownership, risk and environment questions are asked about anything the estate runs or stores, not about one class at a time; the parent is what lets one question or one rule cover all of them.

Component.alternatives: Considered only having System; rejected because it cannot answer what breaks if this is redeployed.
Component.question: What actually gets deployed, and what does it touch?
Component.why: Change and failure happen at the deployable unit, not at the system, so impact questions need this level.

DataStore.question: Where does this data live, and who writes it?
DataStore.why: Two writers to one store is the commonest quiet cause of inconsistency, and it is only visible if the store is a node.

Environment.question: Where does this run, and is the answer the same in production?
Environment.why: Topology differs between environments, and an answer that ignores that is misleading in an incident.

Interface.alternatives: Considered a direct component-to-component dependency; rejected because it hides what the dependency is on.
Interface.question: If we change this, who breaks?
Interface.why: Coupling lives in the contracts others depend on, so the contract must be a node that both sides can point at.

Repository.alternatives: A url attribute on Component. It could not be intended, checked, or acted on as a thing of its own.
Repository.question: Where is the code?
Repository.why: A component without a repository cannot be changed, and an architecture graph that cannot say where the code lives cannot be acted on. Recorded as intended before the repository exists, it is the fact a tool realises.

Runbook.question: How do I operate or recover this at three in the morning?
Runbook.why: The operating procedure is a distinct artifact with its own currency, and it is the thing an incident needs.

System.question: What is this thing, and who owns it?
System.why: A system is the unit people name in conversation and the unit ownership attaches to, so it has to exist even though it is coarse.

WorkItem.question: What is planned, by whom, and what is blocked? (WK1-WK3)
WorkItem.why: The unit the delivery lead plans and the one thing that links the plan to what the product specifies and the estate holds.
WorkItem.alternatives: Epic, Story and Task as classes: rejected, one class with a kind answers the same questions and a story that becomes an epic is a changed attribute, not a changed class.
WorkItem.validated_by: Chiheb Dkhil, 2026-10-07 (B6, the delivery lead's questions)

Milestone.question: What is planned for this milestone? (WK1)
Milestone.why: A release ships; a milestone is reached. Both schedule work, and a demo is not a release.
Milestone.alternatives: Milestone as a kind of Release: rejected, a release is the product's scope boundary and carries what shipped.
Milestone.validated_by: Chiheb Dkhil, 2026-10-07 (B6, the delivery lead's questions)

Transition.question: Where is this item now, and how did it get there? (WK12, WK13)
Transition.why: A state written on an item is overwritten and its history lost; a state appended as a dated, attributed transition keeps every change, lets a merged pull request or a promotion set it the same way a person does, and answers what the state was on any date through the superseded chain.
Transition.alternatives: A `state` attribute set by hand: rejected, no history and no event can set it. A `history` list on the item: rejected, a fact per change is what supersession already does.

Block.question: What is blocked, since when, why, and on whom? (WK11)
Block.why: A blocked item without a reason and someone to ask is a stuck item nobody can unstick. The block carries both, and the shape refuses one without them.
Block.alternatives: Reason and waiting-on as attributes of the item: rejected, they belong to the blocking, not the item, and vanish when it is unblocked. A Block unrelated to Transition: rejected, blocking is a change of state.

Person.question: Whom does a blocked item wait on, and who raised the block? (WK11)
Person.why: A role or a team says what, not who; a block waits on a person who can answer, and a message goes to a person. The communication pack maps a git identity to one.
Person.alternatives: Role only: rejected, the lead asks a person, and the roadmap's notify command needs one.

Message.question: What waits for me, and what was said about this item? (CM1, CM2)
Message.why: A request about a blocked item sent in chat loses the item; sent as a fact beside it, it carries the reason and the date, can be listed when a session opens, and its answer can move the item. Status on the message, not a separate thread class: one fact per message, as everywhere else.
Message.alternatives: Messages outside the graph (email, chat): rejected, the item's context is lost and nothing can be queried. A Thread class: rejected for v1, `regarding` groups them.

cites.question: Which document does this one rest on?
cites.why: A reviewer following a fact to its document often needs the document that one cites; the chain should be walkable in the graph.

acts_on.question: Which entity did this run touch?
acts_on.why: A recorded run is evidence for the facts it asserted about one entity; the edge is how a reader gets from the entity to the run.
acts_on.alternatives: A note in the run record only. Then the entity cannot be asked what was done to it.

executed_by.question: Who is accountable for invoking this?
executed_by.why: A tool that changes the world needs an accountable team, and a reader asking who may run it should find a team, not a person who has since moved.

provides.question: Which product provides this capability?
provides.why: The portfolio's answer to a gap: a capability nothing provides.
provides.alternatives: The estate's `enables` (system to capability): kept beside it; a product provides, its systems enable.

depends_on.question: If this component changes, what else must change?
depends_on.why: Mostly derived by a rule from consumes and exposes; declared so a document that states a dependency outright can be recorded.

member_of.question: Which team does this role sit in?
member_of.why: A role's team is who to page when the holder is away.

about.question: Why is this asset the way it is?
about.why: The product's Decision, widened to the estate, replaces the estate's own DecisionRecord: one record of why, whether it settles scope or a store.
about.alternatives: A separate DecisionRecord with decided_by: rejected on 2026-10-07 because two decision classes in one project is two places to look.

applies_to.alternatives: One constrains relation for both: rejected in the duplicate audit of 2026-09-27.
applies_to.question: Which rules must the product obey, and what is affected? (G6)
applies_to.why: Split from constrains so an agent never confuses a resource limit with a prescribed behaviour that has an authority.

blocks.question: What is still open, and does it stop the release? (C2)
blocks.why: Turns an open question into a release-level fact a gate can check; risks reach a release through threatens, so they were removed from this relation in the duplicate audit.

documented_in.question: Which document says so? (C4)
documented_in.why: Every class except Document is in the domain, because every fact must be citable.

excluded_from.question: What is explicitly out of scope? (B1, failure F1)
excluded_from.why: An explicit exclusion is a fact a builder must see; silence would be read as permission.

exercises.question: How do we test this requirement? (G5)
exercises.why: The edge a test-coverage question runs on: a must requirement with no scenario exercising it is untestable.

in_scope_of.question: What is in scope for the next release? (B1)
in_scope_of.why: Kept separate from excluded_from so absence of an edge means unknown, not out of scope.

interested_in.question: Who must be consulted or informed, and about what? (G3)
interested_in.why: Lets a stakeholder role say what it cares about without a separate Stakeholder class, which decision 1 rejected.

serves.question: Which requirement or journey serves which purpose? (D2)
serves.why: This is the edge the orphan-requirement policy runs on; without it F3 cannot be detected.

governs.question: Which decisions govern this thing? (PR26)
governs.why: A decision that is only `about` something does not say what it changed; `governs` points at the thing that is the way it is because of it, so a reviewer opens a feature or a column and finds the decisions that shaped it.
governs.alternatives: Reuse `about`: rejected, a decision about a product concerns many things and shaped few. An edge from the thing to the decision: rejected, the decision is the one that is written and cites its source.

consumes.question: If we change this interface, who breaks?
consumes.why: This is the edge the impact question runs on, which is why interfaces are modelled at all.

implemented_by.question: Which repository holds this component's code?
implemented_by.why: Change impact ends in code; the edge is how a reader gets from the box to the checkout.

writes_to.alternatives: Considered a single accesses relation; rejected because it cannot answer the question that matters.
writes_to.question: Who writes this store?
writes_to.why: Kept separate from reading so more than one writer is visible as a query rather than as folklore.

satisfies.question: Which requirement does this asset meet, and which requirement does nothing meet?
satisfies.why: The one edge from the design to the specification. With it, the gap between what the product must do and what is built is a query (SA17), not a review meeting.
satisfies.alternatives: A `realises` from Feature (the product's): kept for features; an asset satisfies a requirement directly because a component is not a feature.

delivers.question: Which requirements slip if this component is late? (WK5)
delivers.why: The one edge from the plan to the other levels: an item delivers a requirement, a feature, a component. Without it the plan is a list.
delivers.alternatives: Separate relations per target class: rejected, one question walks them all.
delivers.validated_by: Chiheb Dkhil, 2026-10-07 (B6, the delivery lead's questions)

blocked_by.question: What blocks this item, and whose call is it? (WK3, WK7)
blocked_by.why: A blocker is a thing in the graph (a risk, an open question, a decision, another item), so the question answers who owns it.
blocked_by.validated_by: Chiheb Dkhil, 2026-10-07 (B6, the delivery lead's questions)

scheduled_in.question: What is planned for this milestone or release? (WK1, WK4)
scheduled_in.why: The plan is work placed in time: without the milestone or release an item is scheduled in, no question about a date can run.
scheduled_in.validated_by: Chiheb Dkhil, 2026-10-07 (B6, the delivery lead's questions)

assigned_to.question: What is this team working on? (WK2)
assigned_to.why: Work is done by teams; a role when one function is the point.
assigned_to.validated_by: Chiheb Dkhil, 2026-10-07 (B6, the delivery lead's questions)

transition_of.question: Where is this item now? (WK13)
transition_of.why: The one edge from a change of state to the item it moves; exactly one, or the change moves nothing or two things.
transition_of.alternatives: An item id attribute on the transition: rejected, an edge is what the engine checks and walks.

waiting_on.question: What is blocked, and on whom? (WK11)
waiting_on.why: Whom to tell is the point of recording a block: a person, a team, an item, a decision, a question or a risk, each a thing in the graph that can be asked or watched.
waiting_on.alternatives: Reuse blocked_by: rejected, blocked_by is a standing dependency the plan records and may hold while the item is open; waiting_on is what this block waits on and goes when the block does.

sent_to.question: What waits for this person? (CM1)
sent_to.why: The one edge the inbox walks; a team or role as recipient when anyone of them may answer.
sent_to.alternatives: A `to` string: rejected, a recipient must be a thing in the graph to be asked for its inbox.

sent_by.question: Who asked? (CM2)
sent_by.why: When the project knows the sender as a Person, the edge lets their messages be found; `from` keeps the name as written for the senders it does not.
sent_by.alternatives: Required: rejected for v1, identity arrives with the plugin connection.

regarding.question: What was said about this item? (CM2)
regarding.why: The message's subject, and the block it was sent from, so the reader opens it with the reason and the date beside it.
regarding.alternatives: The item only: rejected, the block holds the reason and goes when it is lifted.

in_reply_to.question: What was answered, and is it settled? (CM2)
in_reply_to.why: A reply is a message like the one it answers, tied to it by one edge; the answered message's status is derived from its replies, so the thread is facts and nobody edits a message.
in_reply_to.alternatives: A status set by hand on the original: rejected, an edited message is not a record. A Reply class: rejected, `outcome` on the reply says what it did.
